summary:
Second Chance is a free browser game that teaches how NASA science missions are designed by letting players fix real missions that failed. Each case follows one loop: watch the real failure, investigate clue cards to find the root cause, redesign the spacecraft, orbit, launcher and tests within six budgets (mass, power, battery, data, money and time), then fly the mission again and make decisions as solar storms and glitches hit.

It answers the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning NASA’s mission design process into play. Up to four players take crew roles, vote Go or No-Go before launch, and verify every requirement with NASA’s four methods: Test, Analysis, Inspection and Demonstration. The cases are real: Vanguard, Mars Climate Orbiter, OCO, Kepler and Swift, plus a new Egyptian satellite mission. Three levels make it work from age 8 to experts, and Orbi, a talking guide, helps players in Arabic and English.

It matters because NASA learns the most from what went wrong, but students rarely get to fix it. Second Chance turns those lessons into an experience anyone can play and remember.
details:
What it does and how it works
Second Chance puts players in the engineer’s seat for NASA missions that failed. Every case follows five steps:

  1. The crash: a short animated scene shows the real failure, narrated by Orbi, our talking guide.
  2. Investigate: players open clue cards (telemetry, reports, design notes) and answer diagnosis questions to find the root cause.
  3. Objective: players choose the science goal, which sets the requirements the mission must meet.
  4. Redesign: players drag parts onto the spacecraft (instruments, power, battery, computer, radio, attitude control), then choose the orbit, launcher and pre-launch tests. Six budget meters (mass, power, battery, data, money and schedule) react live, and the crew votes Go or No-Go before launch.
  5. Fly again: the flight timeline is built from the player’s design. Solar storms, operations problems and glitches force decisions in flight. The mission ends with a report showing telemetry, science data against plan, margins at launch, and a role-by-role teamwork analysis.

The cases are real: Vanguard TV-3 (1957), Mars Climate Orbiter (1999), OCO (2009), Kepler (2012–2013) and Swift (2026). A new case, Eye on the Nile, asks players to design an Egyptian CubeSat from scratch. Two clearly labelled made-up stories for younger players teach real lessons about the lunar night and Mars dust storms.

Benefits and intended impact
Players learn the trade-offs at the heart of systems engineering: margins, interfaces and units, testing, and planning for failure. Every requirement is verified with NASA’s four methods: Test, Analysis, Inspection and Demonstration. Teachers get a report showing each player’s decisions. Arabic and English support, including Orbi’s spoken voice, opens the game to students in Egypt and the wider Arabic-speaking world. Our goal is to make mission design something any student can experience, not just read about.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript in a single page, with no installs and no server. All art is drawn in code with SVG and Canvas. Orbi’s voice uses the browser’s Web Speech API. We used Python for the build script and Playwright to automatically play-test every case and confirm that every challenge at every level can be solved. Claude (Anthropic) assisted with coding and writing, as detailed in our AI disclosure.

Creativity
Most space games let you build anything. Second Chance starts from a real failure, so every decision carries a real lesson. Players act as investigators first and engineers second, using the same kind of evidence NASA’s mishap boards used.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy vs. fun: we simplified the numbers but kept every root cause and lesson as NASA reported it.
  • Age range: three levels. Cadet (8–12) uses pictures and automatic hints, Engineer (13+) uses real numbers, and Flight Director (experts) has strict rules and no hints.
  • Accessibility: it is free, runs in any browser, supports Arabic and English with full right-to-left layout, and Orbi reads text aloud for younger players.
  • Teamwork: up to four players share NASA-style roles and pass the device between them.
  • Honesty: made-up stories are clearly labelled, and every real case links to its NASA source.
